Lectures on Condensed Mathematics Preface This is an updated version of the lectures notes for a course on condensed mathematics taught in the summer term 2019 at the University of Bonn. The material presented is joint work with Dustin Clausen. This is intended as a stable citable version of the original lectures, with mostly cosmetic changes to the original document, together with some small corrections. The content of these lectures has been expanded on at various places, including [ Ásg21 ] , [ Bri25 ] , [ Dég20 ] , [ lS25 ] , [ Mai21 ] , [ Man22 ] , and the reader is strongly encouraged to consider these sources as well. May 2026, Peter Scholze 0.1. Lecture I: Condensed Sets The basic question to be addressed in this course is the following. Question 0.1.1 . How to do algebra when rings/modules/groups carry a topology? This question comes up rather universally, and many solutions have been found so that in any particular situation it is usually clear what to do. Here are some sample situations of interest: (i) Representations of topological groups like GL n ⁡ ( ℝ ) \GL_{n}(\mathbb{R}) , GL n ⁡ ( ℚ p ) \GL_{n}(\mathbb{Q}_{p}) , possibly on Banach spaces or other types of topological vector spaces, or more generally topological abelian groups. (ii) Continuous group cohomology: If G G is a topological group acting on a topological abelian group M M , there are continuous group cohomology groups H cont i ​ ( G , M ) H^{i}_{\mathrm{cont}}(G,M) defined via an explicit cochain complex of continuous cochains. (iii) Algebraic (or rather analytic) geometry over topological fields K K such as ℝ \mathbb{R} or ℚ p \mathbb{Q}_{p} . However, various foundational problems remain, for example: Problems. (i) Topological abelian groups do not form an abelian category. For example, consider the map ( ℝ , discrete ​ topology ) → ( ℝ , natural ​ topology ) . (\mathbb{R},\mathrm{discrete\ topology})\to(\mathbb{R},\mathrm{natural\ topology})\ . In an abelian category, the failure of this map to be an isomorphism has to be explained by a nontrivial kernel or cokernel. Note that this example is not pathological: We certainly want to include all abstract discrete abelian groups, as well as ℝ \mathbb{R} , and we certainly want this map to be a map of topological abelian groups. So if we want to change the setup to obtain an abelian category, we need to include also some kernel or cokernel to the displayed map. (ii) For a topological group G G , a short exact sequence of continuous G G -modules does not in general give long exact sequences of continuous group cohomology groups. More abstractly, the theory of derived categories does not mix well with topological structures. (iii) In the context of analytic geometry over some topological field K K , a theory of quasicoherent sheaves presents problems: For example, if A → B A\to B is a map of topological K K -algebras and M M is a topological A A -module, one would like to form a base change M ​ ⊗ ^ A ​ B M\widehat{\otimes}_{A}B , but it is usually not clear how to complete. The goal of this course is to give a unified approach to the problem of doing algebra when rings/modules/groups/… carry a topology, and resolve those and other foundational problems. The ideas started in this course have been further developed in our joint work with Clausen, see [ Sch20 ] , [ CS22 ] and [ CS26 ] . The solution comes from a somewhat unexpected (to the author) direction. In [ BS15 ] , the pro-étale site X pro ​ e ´ ​ t X_{\mathrm{pro\acute{e}t}} of any scheme X X was defined, whose objects are roughly projective limits of étale maps to X X . For this course, only the simplest case where X X is a (geometric) point is relevant. Indeed, unlike in classical topologies such as the Zariski or étale topology, sheaves on the pro-étale site of a point are not merely sets. What seemed like a bug of the pro-étale site is actually a feature for us here, as Clausen explained to the author. Definition 0.1.2 . The pro-étale site ∗ pro ​ e ´ ​ t \ast_{\mathrm{pro\acute{e}t}} of a point is the category of profinite sets S S , with finite families of jointly surjective maps as covers. A condensed set is a sheaf of sets on ∗ pro ​ e ´ ​ t \ast_{\mathrm{pro\acute{e}t}} . Similarly, a condensed ring/group/… is a sheaf of rings/groups/… on ∗ pro ​ e ´ ​ t \ast_{\mathrm{pro\acute{e}t}} . Generally, if 𝒞 \mathcal{C} is any category, the category Cond ⁡ ( 𝒞 ) \Cond(\mathcal{C}) of condensed objects of 𝒞 \mathcal{C} is the category of 𝒞 \mathcal{C} -valued sheaves on ∗ pro ​ e ´ ​ t \ast_{\mathrm{pro\acute{e}t}} . In other words, a condensed set/ring/group/… is a functor T : { profinite ​ sets } op \displaystyle T:\{\mathrm{profinite\ sets}\}^{\mathrm{op}} → { sets / rings / groups / … } \displaystyle\to\{\mathrm{sets/rings/groups/...}\} S \displaystyle S ↦ T ⁡ ( S ) \displaystyle\mapsto T(S) satisfying T ( ∅ ) = ∗ T(\emptyset)=\ast and the following two conditions (which are equivalent to the sheaf condition): (i) For any profinite sets S 1 , S 2 S_{1},S_{2} , the natural map T ⁡ ( S 1 ⊔ S 2 ) → T ⁡ ( S 1 ) × T ⁡ ( S 2 ) T(S_{1}\sqcup S_{2})\to T(S_{1})\times T(S_{2}) is a bijection. (ii) For any surjection S ′ → S S^{\prime}\to S of profinite sets with the fibre product S ′ × S S ′ S^{\prime}\times_{S}S^{\prime} and its two projections p 1 , p 2 p_{1},p_{2} to S ′ S^{\prime} , the map T ⁡ ( S ) → { x ∈ T ⁡ ( S ′ ) ∣ p 1 ∗ ​ ( x ) = p 2 ∗ ​ ( x ) ∈ T ⁡ ( S ′ × S S ′ ) } T(S)\to\{x\in T(S^{\prime})\mid p_{1}^{\ast}(x)=p_{2}^{\ast}(x)\in T(S^{\prime}\times_{S}S^{\prime})\} is a bijection. Given a condensed set T T , we sometimes refer to T ⁡ ( ∗ ) T(\ast) as its underlying set. The following example presents the key translation from topological structures to condensed structures: Example 0.1.3 . Let T T be any topological space. There is an associated condensed set T ¯ \underline{T} , defined via sending any profinite set S S to the set of continuous maps from S S to T T . This clearly satisfies (i) above, while (ii) follows from the fact that any surjection S ′ → S S^{\prime}\to S of compact Hausdorff spaces is a quotient map, so any map S → T S\to T for which the composite S ′ → S → T S^{\prime}\to S\to T is continuous is itself continuous. If T T is a topological ring/group/…, then T ¯ \underline{T} is a condensed ring/group/… . Remark 0.1.4 . Definition 0.1.2 presents set-theoretic problems: The category of profinite sets is large, so it is not a good idea to consider functors defined on all of it. We will resolve this issue over this and the next lecture, and in doing so we will actually pass to a minor modification of the category above, cf. also Warning 0.2.14 in relation to the previous example. In a first step, we will choose a cardinal bound on the profinite sets, i.e. fix a suitable uncountable cardinal κ \kappa and use only profinite sets S S of cardinality less than κ \kappa to define a site ∗ κ ​ - ​ pro ​ e ´ ​ t \ast_{\kappa\text{-}{\mathrm{pro\acute{e}t}}} . In these lectures, we will always assume that κ \kappa is an uncountable strong limit cardinal, i.e. κ \kappa is uncountable and for all λ < κ \lambda<\kappa , also 2 λ < κ 2^{\lambda}<\kappa . 1 1 1 However, the case of regular κ \kappa is also interesting and useful; in particular, the choice κ = ℵ 1 \kappa=\aleph_{1} leads to the notion of “light condensed sets” which are used in the theory of analytic stacks [ CS26 ] . It is easy to construct such κ \kappa : For example, define ℶ α \beth_{\alpha} inductively for all ordinals α \alpha via ℶ 0 = ℵ 0 \beth_{0}=\aleph_{0} , ℶ α + = 2 ℶ α \beth_{\alpha^{+}}=2^{\beth_{\alpha}} for a successor ordinal and for a limit ordinal as the union of all smaller ℶ α \beth_{\alpha} ’s. Then for any limit ordinal α \alpha , the cardinal κ = ℶ α \kappa=\beth_{\alpha} is an uncountable strong limit cardinal. For any uncountable strong limit cardinal κ \kappa , the category of κ \kappa -condensed sets is the category of sheaves on ∗ κ ​ - ​ pro ​ e ´ ​ t \ast_{\kappa\text{-}{\mathrm{pro\acute{e}t}}} . Remark 0.1.5 . If κ ′ > κ \kappa^{\prime}>\kappa are uncountable strong limit cardinals, there is an obvious forgetful functor from κ ′ \kappa^{\prime} -condensed sets to κ \kappa -condensed sets. This functor admits a natural left adjoint, which is a functor from κ \kappa -condensed sets to κ ′ \kappa^{\prime} -condensed sets. This functor is fully faithful and commutes with all colimits and many limits (in particular, all finite limits), as we will prove in Proposition 0.2.9 below. We will then define the category of condensed sets as the (large) colimit of the category of κ \kappa -condensed sets along the filtered poset of all uncountable strong limit cardinals κ \kappa . 2 2 2 In [ BH19 ] , Barwick–Haine set up closely related foundations, but using different set-theoretic conventions. In particular, they assume the existence of universes, fixing in particular a “tiny” and a “small” universe, and look at sheaves on tiny profinite sets with values in small sets; they term these pyknotic sets. In our language, placing ourselves in the small universe, this would be κ \kappa -condensed sets for the first strongly inaccessible cardinal κ \kappa they consider (the one giving rise to the tiny universe). Recall that a topological space X X is compactly generated if a map f : X → Y f:X\to Y to another topological space Y Y is continuous as soon as the composite S → X → Y S\to X\to Y is continuous for all compact Hausdorff spaces S S mapping to X X . The inclusion of compactly generated spaces into all topological spaces admits a right adjoint X ↦ X cg X\mapsto X^{\mathrm{cg}} that sends a topological space X X to its underlying set equipped with the quotient topology for the map ⊔ S → X S → X \sqcup_{S\to X}S\to X , where the disjoint union runs over all compact Hausdorff spaces S S mapping to X X . Note that any compact Hausdorff space S S admits a surjection from a profinite set (which is then automatically a quotient map), for example by taking the Stone–Čech compactification of S S considered as a discrete set. This means that in the preceding paragraph, one can replace compact Hausdorff spaces by profinite sets without altering the definition of compactly generated spaces and the functor X ↦ X cg X\mapsto X^{\mathrm{cg}} . Warning 0.2.14 , so we are careful with the cardinal bounds here. choose an uncountable strong limit cardinal κ \kappa as above, and say that a topological space X X is κ \kappa -compactly generated if it is equipped with the quotient topology from ⊔ S → X S → X \sqcup_{S\to X}S\to X where now S S runs only over compact Hausdorff spaces with | S | < κ |S|<\kappa . Any compact Hausdorff space S S with | S | < κ |S|<\kappa admits a surjection from the profinite set S ′ S^{\prime} which is the Stone–Čech compactification of S S considered as a discrete set, and then | S ′ | ≤ 2 2 | S | < κ |S^{\prime}|\leq 2^{2^{|S|}}<\kappa as κ \kappa is a strong limit cardinal and S ′ S^{\prime} is the set of ultrafilters on the set S S , i.e. a subset of the powerset of the powerset of S S . We write X ↦ X κ ​ - ​ cg X\mapsto X^{\kappa\text{-}\mathrm{cg}} for the right adjoint of the inclusion of κ \kappa -compactly generated topological spaces into all topological spaces; here X κ ​ - ​ cg X^{\kappa\text{-}\mathrm{cg}} has the underlying set of X X equipped with the quotient topology of ⊔ S → X S → X \sqcup_{S\to X}S\to X where S S runs over κ \kappa -small compact Hausdorff S S . Remark 0.1.6 . Any first-countable topological space X X (in particular, any metrizable topological space) is compactly generated; in fact κ \kappa -compactly generated for any uncountable κ \kappa . Indeed, assume that V ⊂ X V\subset X is a subset such that for all κ \kappa -small compact Hausdorff spaces S S mapping to X X , the preimage of V V in S S is closed. We need to see that V V is closed. Take any point x ∈ X x\in X in the closure of V V , and choose a sequence U 1 ⊃ U 2 ⊃ … U_{1}\supset U_{2}\supset\ldots of cofinal open neighborhoods of x x (using that X X is first-countable). Then V ∩ U n V\cap U_{n} is nonempty for all n n , so choosing a point x n ∈ V ∩ U n x_{n}\in V\cap U_{n} we get a map ℕ ∪ { ∞ } → X \mathbb{N}\cup\{\infty\}\to X sending n n to x n x_{n} and ∞ \infty to x x ; this map is continuous for the usual profinite topology on ℕ ∪ { ∞ } \mathbb{N}\cup\{\infty\} . But then the preimage of V V in ℕ ∪ { ∞ } \mathbb{N}\cup\{\infty\} is closed and contains ℕ \mathbb{N} , and thus also { ∞ } \{\infty\} , so that indeed x ∈ V x\in V , i.e. V V is closed. Proposition 0.1.7 . The functor X ↦ X ¯ X\mapsto\underline{X} from the category of topological spaces/rings/groups/… to the category of κ \kappa -condensed sets/rings/groups/… is faithful, and fully faithful when restricted to the full subcategory of all T T that are κ \kappa -compactly generated as a topological space. The functor X ↦ X ¯ X\mapsto\underline{X} from topological spaces to κ \kappa -condensed sets admits a left adjoint T ↦ T ​ ( ∗ ) top T\mapsto T(\ast)_{\mathrm{top}} sending any condensed set T T to its underlying set T ⁡ ( ∗ ) T(\ast) equipped with the quotient topology of ⊔ S → T S → T ( ∗ ) \sqcup_{S\to T}S\to T(\ast) where the disjoint union runs over all κ \kappa -small profinite sets S S with a map to T T , i.e. an element of T ⁡ ( S ) T(S) . The counit X ¯ ​ ( ∗ ) top → X \underline{X}(\ast)_{\mathrm{top}}\to X of the adjunction agrees with the counit X κ ​ - ​ cg → X X^{\kappa\text{-}\mathrm{cg}}\to X of the adjunction between κ \kappa -compactly generated spaces and all topological spaces; in particular, X ¯ ​ ( ∗ ) top ≅ X κ ​ - ​ cg \underline{X}(\ast)_{\mathrm{top}}\cong X^{\kappa\text{-}\mathrm{cg}} . Remark 0.1.8 . If X X is a condensed group (or ring/…), it is not necessarily the case that X ¯ ​ ( ∗ ) top \underline{X}(\ast)_{\mathrm{top}} is a topological group (or ring/…). The problem is that the functor X ↦ X ​ ( ∗ ) top X\mapsto X(\ast)_{\mathrm{top}} does not necessarily commute with products. Proof. Faithfulness is clear as a map of topological spaces is determined by the underlying map of sets. It suffices to check fully faithfulness for the functor from κ \kappa -compactly generated topological spaces to κ \kappa -condensed sets, as the other cases (of rings and groups) are just certain diagram categories. Here, the claim reduces formally to the claim about the adjoint functor and its counit. Thus, let X X be a topological space and T T a κ \kappa -condensed set. We claim that there is a functorial bijection Hom ⁡ ( T , X ¯ ) = Hom ⁡ ( T ​ ( ∗ ) top , X ) . \Hom(T,\underline{X})=\Hom(T(\ast)_{\mathrm{top}},X)\ . Note that as for all profinite S S , the map X ¯ ​ ( S ) → ∏ s ∈ S X ¯ ​ ( { s } ) = ∏ s ∈ S X \underline{X}(S)\to\prod_{s\in S}\underline{X}(\{s\})=\prod_{s\in S}X is injective (it identifies with the inclusion from the set of continuous maps from S S to X X into all maps from S S to X X ), giving a map T → X ¯ T\to\underline{X} is equivalent to giving a map of sets T ⁡ ( ∗ ) → X T(\ast)\to X such that for all κ \kappa -small profinite S S with a map S → T S\to T , the induced map S → T ⁡ ( ∗ ) → X S\to T(\ast)\to X is continuous. But these are precisely the continuous maps T ​ ( ∗ ) top → X T(\ast)_{\mathrm{top}}\to X by definition of the topology on T ​ ( ∗ ) top T(\ast)_{\mathrm{top}} . It is clear from the definitions that for a topological space X X , there is natural identification X ¯ ​ ( ∗ ) top ≅ X κ ​ - ​ cg \underline{X}(\ast)_{\mathrm{top}}\cong X^{\kappa\text{-}\mathrm{cg}} . ∎ Example 0.1.9 . Let ℝ disc \mathbb{R}_{\mathrm{disc}} denote the real numbers with the discrete topology, and ℝ \mathbb{R} the real numbers with their natural topology. Then the map ℝ disc ¯ → ℝ ¯ \underline{\mathbb{R}_{\mathrm{disc}}}\to\underline{\mathbb{R}} is injective, and its cokernel Q Q is a condensed abelian group with “underlying” abelian group Q ⁡ ( ∗ ) = 0 Q(\ast)=0 . However, for a general profinite set S S , one has Q ( S ) = { continuous maps S → ℝ } / { locally constant maps S → ℝ } ≠ 0 . Q(S)=\{\mathrm{continuous\ maps}\ S\to\mathbb{R}\}/\{\mathrm{locally\ constant\ maps}\ S\to\mathbb{R}\}\neq 0\ . We note that a priori Q Q is the sheafification of this functor, but it turns out that sheafification is unnecessary, by the vanishing H cond 1 ​ ( S , ℝ disc ) = 0 H^{1}_{\mathrm{cond}}(S,\mathbb{R}_{\mathrm{disc}})=0 proved in Theorem 0.3.2 . In fact, condensed abelian groups form an abelian category of the nicest possible sort. In particular, out of Grothendieck’s axioms, it satisfies the same as the category of abelian groups. Theorem 0.1.10 . The category of condensed abelian groups is an abelian category which satisfies Grothendieck’s axioms (AB3), (AB4), (AB5), (AB6), (AB3*) and (AB4*), to wit: all limits (AB3*) and colimits (AB3) exist, arbitrary products (AB4*), arbitrary direct sums (AB4) and filtered colimits (AB5) are exact, and (AB6) for any index set J J and filtered categories I j I_{j} , j ∈ J j\in J , with functors i ↦ M i i\mapsto M_{i} from I j I_{j} to condensed abelian groups, the natural map lim → ( i j ∈ I j ) j ⁡ ∏ j ∈ J M i j → ∏ j ∈ J lim → i j ∈ I j ⁡ M i j \varinjlim_{(i_{j}\in I_{j})_{j}}\prod_{j\in J}M_{i_{j}}\to\prod_{j\in J}\varinjlim_{i_{j}\in I_{j}}M_{i_{j}} is an isomorphism. Moreover, the category of condensed abelian groups is generated by compact projective objects. Recall that an object M M of an abelian category C C is compact if Hom ⁡ ( M , − ) \Hom(M,-) commutes with filtered colimits. Remark 0.1.11 . Sheaves of abelian groups on any site form an abelian category satisfying (AB3), (AB4), (AB5) and (AB3*). However, in almost all cases, they fail (AB4*) and (AB6). These axioms are however a simple consequence of the existence of compact projective generators. In our case, the compact projective generators will come from extremally disconnected sets, as explained in the next lecture. 0.2. Lecture II: Condensed Abelian Groups For a choice of uncountable strong limit cardinal κ \kappa , we made the following definition. Definition 0.2.1 . The site ∗ κ ​ - ​ pro ​ e ´ ​ t \ast_{\kappa\text{-}{\mathrm{pro\acute{e}t}}} is the site of κ \kappa -small profinite sets S S with covers given by finite families of jointly surjective maps. A κ \kappa -condensed set/group/ring/… is a sheaf of sets/groups/rings/… on ∗ κ ​ - ​ pro ​ e ´ ​ t \ast_{\kappa\text{-}{\mathrm{pro\acute{e}t}}} . Today, we prove the following proposition. Theorem 0.2.2 . The category of κ \kappa -condensed abelian groups is an abelian category which satisfies Grothendieck’s axioms (AB3), (AB4), (AB5), (AB6), (AB3*) and (AB4*), to wit: all limits (AB3*) and colimits (AB3) exist, arbitrary products (AB4*), arbitrary direct sums (AB4) and filtered colimits (AB5) are exact, and (AB6) for any index set J J and filtered categories I j I_{j} , j ∈ J j\in J , with functors i ↦ M i i\mapsto M_{i} from I j I_{j} to κ \kappa -condensed abelian groups, the natural map lim → ( i j ∈ I j ) j ⁡ ∏ j ∈ J M i j → ∏ j ∈ J lim → i j ∈ I j ⁡ M i j \varinjlim_{(i_{j}\in I_{j})_{j}}\prod_{j\in J}M_{i_{j}}\to\prod_{j\in J}\varinjlim_{i_{j}\in I_{j}}M_{i_{j}} is an isomorphism. Moreover, the category of κ \kappa -condensed abelian groups is generated by compact projective objects. What makes condensed sets a priori hard to control is the sheaf condition: Forming a colimit requires sheafification, and it is not clear that this can be controlled. In fact, a priori the sheafification involved might range over larger and larger diagrams depending on the choice of κ \kappa . Fortunately, this turns out not to be the case. To prove this, we study two different sites whose categories of sheaves are equivalent to condensed sets. Proposition 0.2.3 . Consider the site of all κ \kappa -small compact Hausdorff spaces, with covers given by finite families of jointly surjective maps. Its category of sheaves is equivalent to κ \kappa -condensed sets via restriction to profinite sets. Proof. For any compact Hausdorff space S S , one can find a profinite S ′ S^{\prime} with a surjection S ′ → S S^{\prime}\to S . For example, one can take for S ′ S^{\prime} the Stone–Čech compactification of S S considered as a discrete set. For any sheaf T T , this determines the value T ⁡ ( S ) T(S) in terms of the values T ⁡ ( S ′ ) T(S^{\prime}) , T ⁡ ( S ′ × S S ′ ) T(S^{\prime}\times_{S}S^{\prime}) on the profinite sets S ′ S^{\prime} , S ′ × S S ′ ⊂ S ′ × S ′ S^{\prime}\times_{S}S^{\prime}\subset S^{\prime}\times S^{\prime} . The desired equivalence follows easily (noting that | S ′ | ≤ 2 2 | S | < κ |S^{\prime}|\leq 2^{2^{|S|}}<\kappa to verify that the cardinal bounds check out). ∎ The Stone–Čech compactifications of discrete sets appearing in the previous proof are actually a very special type of profinite set: Definition 0.2.4 (Gleason, [ Gle58 ] ) . A compact Hausdorff space S S is extremally disconnected if any surjection S ′ → S S^{\prime}\to S from a compact Hausdorff space splits. Example 0.2.5 . Assume that S = β ​ S 0 S=\beta S_{0} is the Stone–Čech compactification of a discrete set S 0 S_{0} . Then S S is extremally disconnected. Indeed, for any surjection S ′ → S S^{\prime}\to S , we may first lift the discrete set S 0 ⊂ S S_{0}\subset S arbitrarily to S ′ S^{\prime} ; this extends to a unique section S = β ​ S 0 → S ′ S=\beta S_{0}\to S^{\prime} by the universal property of the Stone–Čech compactification. In particular, any compact Hausdorff space S S admits a surjection from an extremally disconnected space S ′ = β ​ S S^{\prime}=\beta S , with | S ′ | ≤ 2 2 | S | |S^{\prime}|\leq 2^{2^{|S|}} . Warning 0.2.6 . Being extremally disconnected is a much stronger condition than being totally disconnected, and it is in fact hard to come up with examples that are not Stone–Čech compactifications or very related. (Indeed, any extremally disconnected set is a retract of a Stone–Čech compactification.) In particular, it is known that for two infinite extremally disconnected sets S S , S ′ S^{\prime} , their product S × S ′ S\times S^{\prime} is never extremally disconnected. Also, if S S is extremally disconnected and x 0 , x 1 , … x_{0},x_{1},\ldots is a sequence of points in S S that converges, then it is eventually constant, cf. [ Gle58 ] . Remark 0.2.7 . Extremally disconnected compact Hausdorff spaces play an important role in set theory, or more particularly the theory of forcing, to find interesting models of ZFC. Namely, any extremally disconnected compact Hausdorff space can be used to construct a forcing extension of the ground model, and conversely any forcing extension arises this way. In the language ETCSR of the elementary theory of the category of sets with replacement — which is essentially an equivalent presentation of ZFC, characterizing it in terms of its category of sets, cf. e.g. [ Shu19 ] — the category of sets of the forcing extension is given as follows, cf. [ MLM94 ] . Let S S be an extremally disconnected compact Hausdorff space, and pick a point s ∈ S s\in S . Consider the site of open and closed subsets of S S , where a family { U i ⊂ U } i \{U_{i}\subset U\}_{i} is a cover if ⋃ i U i ⊂ U \bigcup_{i}U_{i}\subset U is dense, and let Shv ∧ ​ ( S ) \mathrm{Shv}^{\wedge}(S) be the resulting category of sheaves. The same construction can be applied to any open and closed subset U ⊂ S U\subset S . One can form the category colim U ∋ s ​ Shv ∧ ​ ( U ) , \mathrm{colim}_{U\ni s}\mathrm{Shv}^{\wedge}(U), where the filtered colimit along the pullback functors is taken in the 2 2 -category of categories. This category turns out to be a model of ETCSR (which can then be reinterpreted as a model of ZFC). If S S is a Stone–Čech compactification, this is simply an ultraproduct of the category Set \mathrm{Set} , and hence passing from Set \mathrm{Set} to this extension does not change the truth of any ZFC-formula. However, for general extremally disconnected profinite sets, this extension is very different. This presentation shows that there is a tight relation between some of the structures of condensed mathematics, and set theory/forcing — both can be seen to be concerned with (different kinds of) sheaves on extremally disconnected spaces. See [ BLH25 ] , [ BB26 ] for very interesting work relating set theory and condensed mathematics. Proposition 0.2.8 . Consider the site of κ \kappa -small extremally disconnected sets, with covers given by finite families of jointly surjective maps. Its category of sheaves is equivalent to κ \kappa -condensed sets via restriction from profinite sets. Proof. For any profinite set S S , we can find an extremally disconnected set S ~ \widetilde{S} surjecting onto S S and another extremally disconnected set S ~ ~ \widetilde{\widetilde{S}} surjecting onto S ~ × S S ~ \widetilde{S}\times_{S}\widetilde{S} . Then the value T ⁡ ( S ) T(S) is determined as the equalizer of the two maps T ⁡ ( S ~ ) → T ⁡ ( S ~ ~ ) T(\widetilde{S})\to T(\widetilde{\widetilde{S}}) . This easily implies the proposition. ∎ Using the proposition, we see that the category of κ \kappa -condensed sets/rings/groups/… is equivalent to the category of functors T : { κ ​ - ​ small ​ extremally ​ disconnected ​ sets } op → { sets / rings / groups / … } T:\{\kappa\text{-}\mathrm{small\ extremally\ disconnected\ sets}\}^{\mathrm{op}}\to\{\mathrm{sets/rings/groups/...}\} such that T ( ∅ ) = ∗ T(\emptyset)=\ast and for all κ \kappa -small extremally disconnected sets S 1 S_{1} , S 2 S_{2} , the natural map T ⁡ ( S 1 ⊔ S 2 ) → T ⁡ ( S 1 ) × T ⁡ ( S 2 ) T(S_{1}\sqcup S_{2})\to T(S_{1})\times T(S_{2}) is a bijection. Indeed, as any cover of extremally disconnected sets splits, the analogue of condition (ii) above is automatic. Proof of Theorem 0.2.2 . We identify the category of κ \kappa -condensed abelian groups with the category of functors M : { κ ​ - ​ small ​ extremally ​ disconnected ​ sets } op → { abelian ​ groups } M:\{\kappa\text{-}\mathrm{small\ extremally\ disconnected\ sets}\}^{\mathrm{op}}\to\{\mathrm{abelian\ groups}\} sending finite disjoint unions to finite products. As the formation of all limits and colimits in the category of abelian groups commutes with finite products (=finite coproducts), one sees that this category is stable under formation of pointwise limits and colimits. In other words, for any category I I and any functor i ↦ M i i\mapsto M_{i} to κ \kappa -condensed abelian groups, the limit (resp. colimit) of i ↦ M i i\mapsto M_{i} is given by sending any κ \kappa -small extremally disconnected set S S to the limit (resp. colimit) of i ↦ M i ​ ( S ) i\mapsto M_{i}(S) . Definition 0.2.11 . The category of condensed sets is given by the filtered colimit of the category of κ \kappa -condensed sets along the filtered poset of all uncountable strong limit cardinals κ \kappa . Remark 0.2.12 .
